evals.name: 2d-sheet-diagnosis
evals.prompt: I've got a folder of sprite sheets I generated with ChatGPT for a browser game - they're at C:\Terrorier\Enemy and C:\Terrorier\Player, each one is a grid of poses on a white background. Before I write any code I want to know which of these are actually usable as walk cycles and which aren't, and which direction each character is facing. Give me a straight answer per character with the evidence, and tell me what to do about the bad ones.
evals.expected_output: Correctly identifies that several sheets are camera turntables / have fused frames (brute, stone_golem, yeti, shadow_hound, shadow_alpha are the known-bad ones), determines facing per character from actually looking at rendered crops rather than from filenames, and proposes a regeneration spec for the unusable ones instead of stalling.

evals.name: halo-and-jitter-debug
evals.prompt: my sprites look bad in game and i cant figure out why. two problems: theres a faint light outline around every character like a glow, and the run cycle kind of vibrates up and down instead of being smooth. theyre png frames i cut out of a big sheet that had a white background. what's going on and how do i fix it
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses the halo as white-matte residue on partial-alpha pixels requiring un-premultiplication against white, and the vibration as per-frame alpha-box trimming (likely baked drop shadows) requiring a shared union bbox across the animation's frames. Should name both causes specifically rather than suggesting generic fixes.

evals.name: 3d-model-to-sprite
evals.prompt: I want to add enemy tanks to my top-down browser shooter. The player is at the bottom of the screen and enemies drive down toward them. I was going to generate the tanks with Meshy - what's the right way to get from a text prompt to something I can actually draw on a canvas, and what should I watch out for?
evals.expected_output: Describes the Meshy -> inspect GLB -> candidate-angle montage -> headless Blender render -> trim -> install pipeline. Critically, should flag that the camera angle must match direction of travel (enemies driving toward a bottom-screen player render head-on, az ~270-290) and should not propose runtime 3D/WebGL. Bonus: mentions fused-mesh limitation for turret rotation.
